source_refs.note: Practice long questions written from Chapter 3 (PDF 54-74, printed 51-71); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 3 (Circular and Rotational Motion), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define angular displacement and the radian. Show that S = rθ and that one revolution is 2π rad. Also define average and instantaneous angular velocity and give its unit and direction. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Setting: A particle P of mass m moves on a circle of radius r at the end of a massless rigid rod OP pivoted at the centre O (Fig. 3.2). The axis of rotation passes through O, normal to the plane of rotation (z-axis); x and y lie in the plane of rotation.

Angular displacement: At time t, OP is at OP₁ making angle θ with the x-axis; at t + Δt it is at OP₂ making θ + Δθ. The angle Δθ is the angular displacement of OP during Δt. It is positive for counter clockwise rotation. For very small Δθ it is a vector along the axis of rotation, given by the right hand rule: grasp the axis in the right hand with fingers curling in the direction of rotation; the thumb points in the direction of angular displacement.

Radian: If the arc AB of a circle equals the radius r, the angle at the centre is one radian (rad), the SI unit of angle.
For an arc of length S subtending angle θ at the centre (Fig. 3.3):
θ = S/r, or S = rθ (θ in radian) ... (3.1)

One revolution: In one revolution P covers S = 2πr, so
θ = S/r = 2πr/r = 2π
1 revolution = 2π rad = 360°, and 1 rad = 360°/2π = 57.3°

Angular velocity: the rate at which angular displacement changes with time.
Average: ω_av = Δθ/Δt ... (3.2)
Instantaneous: ω = lim (Δt → 0) Δθ/Δt ... (3.3)
In this limit Δθ is infinitesimally small and a vector, so ω is also a vector, directed along the axis of rotation by the right hand rule.
Unit: rad s⁻¹ (SI); also revolution per minute (rpm).

book_ref.quote: Consider the motion of a single particle P of mass m in a circular path of radius r.

blocks.prompt: 2 A wheel turns uniformly at 450 rpm. Find (i) its angular velocity in rad s⁻¹ (ii) the angle it turns through in 2.0 s, in radians and revolutions (iii) the arc length covered in this time by a point 0.25 m from the axis. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert rpm to rev s⁻¹ and then to rad s⁻¹; θ = ωt for uniform rotation; S = rθ with θ in radian.

book_ref.quote: Angular velocity is measured in radians per second which is the SI unit.

steps: ω = 450 rev/min × 2π rad/rev ÷ 60 s/min = 15π rad s⁻¹ = 47.1 rad s⁻¹
θ = ωt = 47.1 rad s⁻¹ × 2.0 s = 94.2 rad
In revolutions: θ = 94.2/2π = 15 rev (check: 7.5 rev s⁻¹ × 2.0 s = 15 rev)
blocks.final_answer: ω = 47.1 rad s⁻¹; θ = 94.2 rad = 15 rev; S = 23.6 m

blocks.prompt: 3 Define average and instantaneous angular acceleration and give their unit and direction. Explain how the rotation of a rigid body is described by its reference line, and write the equations of angular motion with their linear counterparts, stating when they hold. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Angular acceleration: the rate of change of angular velocity (e.g. a fan just switched on). If the angular velocity is ωᵢ at tᵢ and ω_f at t_f:
α_av = (ω_f − ωᵢ)/(t_f − tᵢ) = Δω/Δt ... (3.4)
Instantaneous: α = lim (Δt → 0) Δω/Δt ... (3.5)
It is a vector along the axis of rotation; unit rad s⁻².

Reference line: For a rigid body (Fig. 3.4), the perpendicular OP from a point P of the body to the axis is the reference line. As the body rotates, OP rotates with the same angular velocity and angular acceleration, so the rotation of the rigid body is described by the rotation of OP.

Equations of angular motion: Eqs. 3.2-3.5 are exactly analogous to the linear ones with S, v and a replaced by θ, ω and α. The other linear equations were obtained by algebra from these, so analogous angular equations follow:
Linear: vf = vi + at → Angular: ωf = ωi + αt ... (3.9)
Linear: 2aS = vf² − vi² → Angular: 2αθ = ωf² − ωi² ... (3.10)
Linear: S = vit + ½at² → Angular: θ = ωit + ½αt² ... (3.11)

Condition: these hold only when the axis of rotation is fixed, so that all angular vectors have the same direction and can be manipulated as scalars.

book_ref.quote: As the other equations of linear motion were obtained by algebraic manipulation of these equations

blocks.prompt: 4 A ceiling fan is switched on and its angular velocity rises uniformly from zero to 4.0 rev s⁻¹ in 8.0 s. Find its angular acceleration (in rev s⁻² and rad s⁻²) and the number of revolutions it makes in this time. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use ωf = ωi + αt for α, then θ = ωit + ½αt²; check with 2αθ = ωf² − ωi².

book_ref.quote: When we switch on an electric fan, we notice that its angular velocity goes on increasing.

steps: ωi = 0, ωf = 4.0 rev s⁻¹, t = 8.0 s
blocks.final_answer: α = 0.50 rev s⁻² = 3.14 rad s⁻²; 16 revolutions

blocks.prompt: 5 Derive the relation between the linear (tangential) velocity of a point of a rotating rigid body and the angular velocity. Why is this velocity called tangential? Also write the relation between tangential and angular acceleration and explain what these relations show. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Consider a rigid body rotating about the z-axis with angular velocity ω (Fig. 3.5 a). A point P is at perpendicular distance r from the axis; OP is the reference line. P moves on a circle of radius r with linear velocity v while OP rotates with ω. The axis is fixed, so ω is treated as a scalar, and only the magnitude of v is considered.

In time Δt, P moves through arc P₁P₂ = ΔS while OP turns through Δθ radian (Fig. 3.5 b). By Eq. 3.1:
ΔS = r Δθ
Dividing by Δt:
ΔS/Δt = r Δθ/Δt ... (3.6)
In the limit Δt → 0, ΔS/Δt is the speed v of P on the circle and Δθ/Δt is the angular velocity ω of OP:
v = rω ... (3.7)

Tangential velocity: as Δt → 0 the arc P₁P₂ becomes very small and its direction is the tangent at P₁. So the velocity of P always points along the tangent to the circle; it is called the tangential velocity.

Accelerations: if OP has angular acceleration α, P has a tangential acceleration aₜ; from Eq. 3.7:
aₜ = rα ... (3.8)

Meaning: points at different distances from the axis do not have the same speed or acceleration, but all points of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis have the same angular displacement, angular speed and angular acceleration at any instant. So angular variables describe the motion of the whole body simply.

book_ref.quote: Suppose during the course of its motion, the point P moves through a distance P₁P₂ = ΔS

blocks.prompt: 6 The angular velocity of a disc of radius 0.20 m increases uniformly from 10 rad s⁻¹ to 30 rad s⁻¹ in 4.0 s. Find (i) its angular acceleration (ii) the tangential acceleration of a point on the rim (iii) the linear speed of that point at the start and at the end. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find α from the change of ω, then use aₜ = rα and v = rω.

book_ref.quote: Using Eq. 3.7 it can be shown that the two accelerations are related by

steps: aₜ = rα = 0.20 m × 5.0 rad s⁻² = 1.0 m s⁻²
blocks.final_answer: α = 5.0 rad s⁻²; aₜ = 1.0 m s⁻²; speed 2.0 m s⁻¹ → 6.0 m s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 7 What is centripetal force? Explain why a body moving in a circle with uniform speed needs it, give its direction and expression, and name the agencies that provide it in different motions. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Force and velocity: by Newton's second law a force produces acceleration in its own direction. A force along the velocity changes only the speed, keeping the direction unchanged. A constant force perpendicular to the velocity of a body moving in a circle changes only the direction; the speed remains the same.

Need: a ball whirled on a string in a horizontal circle (Fig. 3.6 a) would not continue in the circle if the string snapped; at point A it would follow the straight line AB, the tangent at A (Fig. 3.6 b). So a force is needed to change the direction of motion continuously at each point.

Definition: The force needed to bend the straight path of a particle into a circular path is called the centripetal (centre seeking) force.

Direction: it does not alter the speed, only the direction; it acts along the radius, always towards the centre, perpendicular to the tangential velocity at each point.

Expression: for mass m moving with speed v on a circle of radius r:
F꜀ = ma꜀ = mv²/r ... (3.12)
where a꜀ = v²/r is the centripetal acceleration towards the centre. As v = rω:
F꜀ = mrω² ... (3.13)

Agencies:
1. Ball whirled on a string: tension in the string.
2. Object on a turntable: friction.
3. Earth around the Sun, Moon and satellites around the Earth: gravitational force.
4. Charged particle: a perpendicular magnetic force.
5. Vehicle on a turn: friction between tyres and road; at high speed on a slippery road this may not suffice, so roads are banked (outer edge slightly higher).

book_ref.quote: Newton's second law of motion states that when a force acts on a body, it produces acceleration in the same direction.

blocks.prompt: 8 A coin of mass 20 g lies 10 cm from the centre of a turntable that turns at 60 rpm. Find the angular velocity, the centripetal acceleration of the coin and the friction force needed to keep it in place. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Friction supplies the centripetal force; find ω from rpm, then a꜀ = rω² and F꜀ = ma꜀.

book_ref.quote: For an object placed on a turntable, the friction is the centripetal force.

steps: ω = 60 rev/min × 2π ÷ 60 s = 2π rad s⁻¹ = 6.28 rad s⁻¹
This force is supplied by friction between the coin and the turntable.
blocks.final_answer: ω = 6.28 rad s⁻¹; a꜀ = 3.95 m s⁻²; friction = 0.079 N

blocks.prompt: 9 A ball tied to a string is whirled in a vertical circle of radius r. Find the tension in the string at the highest point when the speed there is v. What is the condition for the tension to be zero there? Use the result to explain why water does not fall from a bucket whirled rapidly in a vertical circle. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Situation: a ball of mass m on a string moves in a vertical circle of radius r under gravity (Fig. 3.7). At the highest point A its speed is v.

Forces at A: two forces act on the ball, the pull of the string T and the weight w = mg. Both act along the radius at A, towards the centre O. For the ball to travel in the circle, their vector sum must furnish the required centripetal force:
T + w = mv²/r
As w = mg:
T = mv²/r − mg = m(v²/r − g)

Zero tension: if v²/r = g, then T = 0 and the centripetal force is just equal to the weight. The speed at the top for this is v = √(gr).

Bucket of water: at the top the water also needs a centripetal force mv²/r towards the centre. When the bucket is whirled rapidly, mv²/r is not less than the weight mg; the weight together with the push of the bucket's bottom is fully used in keeping the water moving on the circle. So the water stays pressed against the bucket and does not fall, even when the bucket is upside down.

book_ref.quote: For the ball to travel in a circle, the force acting on the ball must provide the required centripetal force.

blocks.prompt: 10 A 0.20 kg ball on a string 0.80 m long is whirled in a vertical circle. Find the tension in the string at the highest point when the ball's speed there is 4.0 m s⁻¹. What is the least speed at the top for which the string stays just taut? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: At the top T + mg = mv²/r, so T = m(v²/r − g); the string just goes slack when T = 0, i.e. v = √(gr).

book_ref.quote: If v²/r = g, then T will be zero and the centripetal force is just equal to the weight.

steps: Least speed: T = 0 when v²/r = g
blocks.final_answer: T = 2.04 N ≈ 2.0 N; least speed at the top = 2.8 m s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 11 What are artificial satellites? Derive the critical velocity of a satellite orbiting close to the Earth and the period of its revolution. How do the speed and period change for a satellite much higher above the Earth? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Artificial satellites: objects that orbit in a nearly circular path around the Earth. They are put into orbit by rockets and held in orbit by the Earth's gravitational pull. Without this pull they would fly off along the tangent to the orbit. (Newton predicted them: an object thrown horizontally with a particular speed from a sufficiently high place would start revolving around the Earth.)

Critical velocity: a low flying satellite has acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻² towards the Earth's centre. Moving in a circle, its acceleration is v²/r. In a circular orbit gravity supplies the centripetal acceleration:
g = v²/R ... (3.14)
where R is the Earth's radius (6400 km). So
v = √(gR) = √(9.8 m s⁻² × 6.4 × 10⁶ m) = 7.9 × 10³ m s⁻¹ = 7.9 km s⁻¹
This is the minimum velocity necessary to put a satellite into orbit, the critical velocity.

Period:
T = 2πR/v = 2 × 3.14 × 6400 km / 7.9 km s⁻¹ = 5088 s ≈ 85 min
(book correction: the printed 5060 s should be 5088 s).

Higher satellites: at a height h much greater than R, the gravitational acceleration decreases inversely as the square of the distance from the Earth's centre. The higher the satellite, the slower the required speed and the longer it takes to complete one revolution.

book_ref.quote: Satellites are objects that orbit in nearly circular path around the Earth.

blocks.prompt: 12 A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 6.8 × 10⁶ m, where the gravitational acceleration is 8.7 m s⁻². Find its orbital speed and its period in minutes. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Gravity at the orbit supplies the centripetal acceleration: g = v²/r gives v; then T = 2πr/v.

book_ref.quote: When the satellite is moving in a circle, it has an acceleration v²/r.

steps: T = 5555 s ÷ 60 = 92.6 min (longer than about 85 min for a satellite close to the Earth)

blocks.prompt: 13 Derive an expression for the orbital speed of a satellite revolving around the Earth in a circular orbit of radius r. Show that it does not depend on the satellite's mass, and explain what happens if the satellite's speed is less than this value. How is the period found? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Let a satellite of mass mₛ move with orbital speed v in a circular orbit of radius r around the Earth of mass M (Fig. 3.12).

Required centripetal force: mₛv²/r.
This force is provided by the gravitational force of attraction between the Earth and the satellite, GmₛM/r². Equating:
GmₛM/r² = mₛv²/r
Cancelling mₛ and one r:
v² = GM/r
v = √(GM/r) ... (3.15)

Mass of satellite: mₛ cancels, so the mass of the satellite is unimportant in describing its orbit. Any satellite orbiting at distance r from the Earth's centre must have the orbital speed of Eq. 3.15.

Smaller speed: any speed less than this will bring the satellite tumbling back to the Earth.

Period: the satellite covers 2πr in one revolution, so T = 2πr/v, where r = R + h for a satellite at height h above the Earth's surface (Example 3.4).

book_ref.quote: Figure 3.12 shows a satellite going round the Earth in a circular path.

blocks.prompt: 14 A satellite revolves in a circular orbit 1600 km above the Earth's surface. Find its orbital speed and period. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6400 km) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Measure the orbit radius from the Earth's centre (r = R + h), use v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v.

book_ref.quote: Take mass of the Earth M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and its radius R = 6400 km.

blocks.prompt: 15 Explain why bodies and astronauts inside an orbiting satellite experience weightlessness. Show mathematically that the supporting force on a body inside the satellite is zero. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reason: everything inside an orbiting satellite experiences weightlessness because the satellite is accelerating towards the centre of the Earth as a freely falling body.

Proof: consider a satellite of mass M in an orbit of radius r. A body of mass m hangs from a spring balance on the ceiling (Fig. 3.13). Two forces act on it: its weight mg downward (towards the Earth) and the supporting force F_N (tension of the spring) upward. Their resultant is the centripetal force needed by m towards the Earth's centre:
F꜀ = mg − F_N ... (3.16)
with F꜀ = mv²/r:
mv²/r = mg − F_N ... (3.16-a)

The centripetal force for the satellite itself is provided by gravity:
F_g = F꜀, so Mg = Mv²/r, giving g = v²/r
Putting v²/r = g in Eq. 3.16-a:
mg = mg − F_N, or F_N = 0

Result: the supporting force on a body inside the satellite is zero, so the spring balance reads zero. Bodies and astronauts in a satellite are therefore in a state of apparent weightlessness; gravity still acts and supplies the centripetal force.

book_ref.quote: Consider a satellite of mass M revolving in its orbit of radius r around the Earth.

blocks.prompt: 16 A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m where the gravitational acceleration is 8.2 m s⁻². A 2.0 kg mass hangs from a spring balance inside it. Find (i) the speed of the satellite (ii) the centripetal force needed by the mass and its weight there (iii) the reading of the balance. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Gravity gives the satellite's centripetal acceleration (g = v²/r); then use mv²/r = mg − F_N for the hanging mass.

book_ref.quote: Their resultant force is equal to the centripetal force required by the mass m

steps: Weight at the orbit: mg = 2.0 × 8.2 = 16.4 N
blocks.final_answer: v = 7.58 km s⁻¹; both forces 16.4 N; balance reads zero

blocks.prompt: 17 What is artificial gravity and why is it needed in a spaceship? Derive the frequency with which a spaceship of outer radius R must rotate to provide gravity like that of the Earth. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Need: in gravity free space no force pushes anybody to any side of the spacecraft. Over an extended stay in orbit, weightlessness may affect the performance of astronauts. Artificial gravity lets the crew function in an almost normal manner.

How: the spaceship is set into rotation about its own axis. The astronaut is pressed towards the outer rim and exerts a force on the 'floor' as on the Earth; the surface of the rotating ship pushes on him and provides the centripetal force.

Derivation: let the outer radius be R and the angular speed ω (Fig. 3.14). The centripetal acceleration of a point on the outer rim is
a꜀ = Rω²
(book correction: this is a centripetal, not an angular, acceleration).
But ω = 2π/t, where t is the period of revolution:
a꜀ = R(2π)²/t² = R 4π²/t²
As frequency f = 1/t:
a꜀ = R 4π² f²
f² = a꜀/(4π²R), or f = (1/2π)√(a꜀/R)
For Earth-like gravity, a꜀ = g:
f = (1/2π)√(g/R) ... (3.17)

When the spaceship rotates with this frequency, inhabitants get artificial gravity like the Earth's.

book_ref.quote: In a gravity free space, there will be no force that will push anybody to any side of the spacecraft.

blocks.prompt: 18 A wheel-shaped spaceship has an outer radius of 150 m. Find the frequency, period and angular speed with which it must rotate to give Earth-like gravity (g = 9.8 m s⁻²) at its rim. What is the speed of a point on the rim? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use f = (1/2π)√(g/R); then t = 1/f, ω = 2πf and v = Rω.

book_ref.quote: The outer radius of the spaceship is R and it rotates around its own central axis with angular speed

blocks.prompt: 19 Define moment of inertia. Starting from F = ma for a single mass on a massless rod, show that τ = Iα, and extend the result to a rigid body to obtain I = Σmᵢrᵢ². (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Single mass: a mass m is fixed at the end of a massless rod pivoted at O on a frictionless bearing, in a horizontal plane (Fig. 3.15). A force F acts on the mass perpendicular to the rod:
F = ma
The mass rotates about O; its tangential acceleration is related to angular acceleration by a_T = rα, so
F = mrα
Turning effect is produced by torque, so multiply both sides by r:
rF = τ = mr²α
This is the rotational analogue of F = ma: F is replaced by τ, a by α and m by mr².

Moment of inertia: the quantity mr² is the moment of inertia I. It plays the same role in angular motion as mass in linear motion, and depends not only on m but also on r².

Rigid body: the body is made of small masses m₁, m₂, ..., mₙ at distances r₁, r₂, ..., rₙ from the axis (Fig. 3.16). Torques:
τ₁ = m₁r₁²α, τ₂ = m₂r₂²α, and so on
(the body is rigid, so all masses have the same α). Total torque:
τ_total = (m₁r₁² + m₂r₂² + ... + mₙrₙ²)α = (Σmᵢrᵢ²)α
τ = Iα ... (3.18)
where I = Σmᵢrᵢ² ... (3.19) is the moment of inertia of the body (unit kg m²).

book_ref.quote: Consider a mass m attached to the end of a massless rod as shown in Fig. 3.15.

blocks.prompt: 20 Two small masses, 2.0 kg at 0.50 m and 3.0 kg at 0.80 m from the axis, are fixed on a light rod. Find (i) the moment of inertia of the system (ii) the torque needed to give it an angular acceleration of 4.0 rad s⁻² (iii) the time this torque takes to bring it from rest to 20 rad s⁻¹. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Add mr² for each mass; τ = Iα; then ωf = ωi + αt.

book_ref.quote: As shown in Fig. 3.16(a), the rigid body is made up of n small pieces of masses

blocks.prompt: 21 Define angular momentum of a particle and give its magnitude, direction and SI unit. Show that for a particle in a circle L = mr²ω, and that for a symmetric rigid body rotating about a fixed axis L = Iω. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: a particle possesses angular momentum about a reference axis if its angular position changes relative to that axis. For a particle of mass m, velocity v and momentum p, about origin O:
L = r × p ... (3.20)
where r is the position vector of the particle relative to O.

Magnitude: L = rp sin θ = mrv sin θ, where θ is the angle between r and p.
Direction: perpendicular to the plane of r and p, sense by the right hand rule of vector product.
SI unit: kg m² s⁻¹ or J s.

Particle in a circle: moving in a circle of radius r with uniform ω, the angle between r and the tangential velocity is 90°:
L = mrv sin 90° = mrv
But v = rω, hence L = mr²ω

Rigid body: a symmetric rigid body rotates about a fixed axis through its centre of mass (Fig. 3.17). Each particle moves in a circle with the same ω. For the ith particle, Lᵢ = mᵢvᵢrᵢ, in the direction of ω; with vᵢ = rᵢω, Lᵢ = mᵢrᵢ²ω. Summing over all particles:
L = (Σmᵢrᵢ²)ω = Iω
where I is the moment of inertia of the body about the axis of rotation.

book_ref.quote: The angular momentum L of a particle of mass m moving with velocity v and momentum p

blocks.prompt: 22 A 0.50 kg ball is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 1.2 m at 3.0 rev s⁻¹. Find its angular velocity, its angular momentum using L = mr²ω, and check the result with L = mvr. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert rev s⁻¹ to rad s⁻¹, use L = mr²ω, and check with v = rω and L = mvr.

book_ref.quote: If the particle is moving in a circle of radius r with uniform angular velocity

steps: Check: L = mvr = 0.50 × 22.6 × 1.2 = 13.6 kg m² s⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: ω = 18.8 rad s⁻¹; L = 13.6 kg m² s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 23 State the law of conservation of angular momentum and show that I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ for a spinning body that changes its moment of inertia. Explain with three examples, and explain why the axis of rotation keeps a fixed direction. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Law: if no external torque acts on a system, the total angular momentum of the system remains constant:
L_total = L₁ + L₂ + ... = constant
It is a fundamental principle, verified from the cosmological to the sub microscopic level.

Changing moment of inertia: a body of moment of inertia I₁ spinning at ω₁ alters its moment of inertia to I₂; with no external torque its angular momentum stays constant (L = Iω), so ω changes to ω₂:
I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂
Decreasing I increases ω, and increasing I decreases ω.

Examples:
1. Diver: after leaving the springboard he curls in arms and legs, I decreases and he spins with a large ω; before touching the water he stretches out, ω decreases and he enters gently.
2. Ice skater: folding the arms and bringing the stretched leg in decreases I and increases ω; stretching out increases I and decreases ω.
3. Man on a turntable with dumb-bells: drawing the hands in decreases I, so the angular speed at once increases.
(Also: when polar ice melts and flows away, the Earth's I increases, ω decreases and the day becomes longer.)

Fixed axis: angular momentum is a vector along the axis of rotation, so its direction also stays fixed. The axis of rotation of an object will not change its orientation unless an external torque causes it to do so. The major force on the Earth is the Sun's pull, giving no sizeable torque, so the Earth's axis stays fixed in one direction.

book_ref.quote: The law of conservation of angular momentum is one of the fundamental principles of Physics.

blocks.prompt: 24 An ice skater spins at 1.5 rev s⁻¹ with arms outstretched, with moment of inertia 4.0 kg m². She folds her arms and her moment of inertia becomes 1.6 kg m². Find her new rate of spin and her angular momentum. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: No external torque, so I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂; angular momentum L = Iω with ω in rad s⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: If a body of moment of inertia I₁, spinning with angular speed

blocks.final_answer: ω₂ = 3.75 rev s⁻¹; L = 37.7 kg m² s⁻¹
